paragraphs: But Balaam’s ass had suddenly spoken. The subject was a strange one. Grigory had gone out that morning to do some shopping, and the shopkeeper Lukyanov had told him a story about a Russian soldier, which had appeared in that day’s newspaper. This soldier had been taken prisoner somewhere in a remote part of Asia. He was threatened with instant, agonizing death unless he gave up Christianity and converted to Islam. He refused to deny his faith. He was tortured and flayed alive, and he died praising and glorifying Christ. Grigory had told the story at table. Fyodor Pavlovitch always liked to laugh and chat over dessert after dinner, even if only with Grigory. This afternoon he was in an especially good mood, and in a talkative one. Sipping his brandy and listening to the story, he remarked that they ought to make a saint of a soldier like that and send his skin to some monastery. “That would make the people flock there, and bring the money in.”

Grigory frowned. He could see that Fyodor Pavlovitch was not in the least touched, but was starting, as usual, to scoff. At that moment Smerdyakov, who was standing by the door, smiled. Smerdyakov often waited at table toward the end of dinner, and since Ivan’s arrival in our town he had done so every day.
“What are you grinning at?” asked Fyodor Pavlovitch, who had caught the smile at once and knew it was meant for Grigory.

“Well, my opinion is,” Smerdyakov began suddenly, in a loud voice that nobody expected, “that if that praiseworthy soldier’s deed was so very great, then there would have been, to my way of thinking, no sin in it if he had, in such an emergency, renounced, so to speak, the name of Christ and his own christening, in order to save his life by that means, and so to do good deeds with it, and in the course of years make up for his cowardice.”
“How could it not be a sin? You’re talking nonsense. For that you’ll go straight to hell and be roasted there like mutton,” put in Fyodor Pavlovitch.
It was at this point that Alyosha came in, and Fyodor Pavlovitch, as we have seen, was delighted to see him.
“We’re on your subject, your subject,” he chuckled gleefully, and made Alyosha sit down to listen.
“As for mutton, that’s not so, and there’ll be nothing of the kind there for this, and there shouldn’t be either, if it’s done according to justice,” Smerdyakov maintained stoutly.
“What do you mean, ‘according to justice’?” Fyodor Pavlovitch cried, more cheerful still, and nudged Alyosha with his knee.
“He’s a rascal, that’s what he is!” burst from Grigory. He looked Smerdyakov angrily in the face.

“As for being a rascal, wait a little, Grigory Vassilyevitch,” answered Smerdyakov, perfectly calm. “You had better think about it yourself. Suppose I am taken prisoner by the enemies of the Christian race, and they demand that I curse the name of God and renounce my holy christening. I am fully entitled to act by my own reason, since there would be no sin in it.”
“But you’ve said that already. Don’t waste words. Prove it,” cried Fyodor Pavlovitch.
“Soup-maker!” muttered Grigory with contempt.

“As for being a soup-maker, wait a bit with that too, and think it over for yourself, Grigory Vassilyevitch, without abusing me. For the moment I say to those enemies, ‘No, I’m not a Christian, and I curse my true God,’ then at once, by God’s high judgment, I become, immediately and specially, anathema accursed, and I am cut off from the Holy Church, exactly as if I were a heathen. So at that very instant, not only when I say it aloud but when I merely think of saying it, before a quarter of a second has passed, I am cut off. Is that so or not, Grigory Vassilyevitch?”
He addressed Grigory with obvious satisfaction. Really he was answering Fyodor Pavlovitch’s questions, and he knew it, and he was deliberately pretending that Grigory had asked them.
“Ivan,” cried Fyodor Pavlovitch suddenly, “bend down so I can whisper to you. He’s got all this up for your benefit. He wants you to praise him. Praise him.”
Ivan listened to his father’s excited whisper with perfect seriousness.
“Wait, Smerdyakov, be quiet a minute,” cried Fyodor Pavlovitch once more. “Ivan, your ear again.”
Ivan bent down again, with a perfectly grave face.
“I love you as I do Alyosha. Don’t think I don’t love you. Some brandy?”
“Yes.—But you’re rather drunk yourself,” thought Ivan, looking steadily at his father.
He was watching Smerdyakov with great curiosity.
“You’re anathema accursed already, as it is,” Grigory suddenly burst out, “and how dare you argue after that, you rascal, if—”
“Don’t scold him, Grigory, don’t scold him,” Fyodor Pavlovitch cut him short.

“You should wait, Grigory Vassilyevitch, even a short time, and listen, for I haven’t finished what I had to say. At the very moment I become accursed, at that same highest moment, I become exactly like a heathen, and my christening is taken off me and counts for nothing. Isn’t that so?”
“Hurry up and finish, my boy,” Fyodor Pavlovitch urged him, sipping from his wine-glass with relish.

“And if I’ve stopped being a Christian, then I told no lie to the enemy when they asked whether I was a Christian or not a Christian. I had already been relieved of my Christianity by God Himself, by reason of the thought alone, before I had time to say a word to the enemy. And if I have already been discharged, then how, and with what sort of justice, can I be held responsible as a Christian in the other world for having denied Christ? Through the very thought alone, before denying Him, I had been relieved of my christening. If I’m no longer a Christian, then I can’t renounce Christ, for then I’ve nothing to renounce. Who will hold an unclean Tatar responsible, Grigory Vassilyevitch, even in heaven, for not having been born a Christian? And who would punish him for that, considering that you can’t take two skins off one ox? For God Almighty Himself, even if He did hold the Tatar responsible, would give him, when he dies, the smallest possible punishment, I imagine (since he must be punished). He would judge that the Tatar is not to blame if he has come into the world an unclean heathen, born of heathen parents. The Lord God surely can’t take a Tatar and say he was a Christian? That would mean that the Almighty would tell a real untruth. And can the Lord of Heaven and earth tell a lie, even in one word?”

Grigory was thunderstruck. He stared at the orator, his eyes nearly starting out of his head. He did not clearly understand what had been said, but he had caught something in this rigmarole, and he stood there looking like a man who has just hit his head against a wall. Fyodor Pavlovitch emptied his glass and burst into his shrill laugh.

“Alyosha! Alyosha! What do you say to that! Ah, you casuist! He must have been with the Jesuits somewhere, Ivan. Oh, you stinking Jesuit, who taught you? But you’re talking nonsense, you casuist, nonsense, nonsense, nonsense. Don’t cry, Grigory, we’ll reduce him to smoke and ashes in a moment. Tell me this, you ass: you may be right before your enemies, but you have renounced your faith all the same in your own heart, and you say yourself that in that very hour you became anathema accursed. And once you’re anathema, they won’t pat you on the head for it in hell. What do you say to that, my fine Jesuit?”
“There is no doubt that I have renounced it in my own heart, but there was no special sin in that. Or if there was a sin, it was the most ordinary one.”
“How’s that, the most ordinary?”
“You lie, accursed one!” hissed Grigory.

“Think it over yourself, Grigory Vassilyevitch,” Smerdyakov went on, steady and unruffled, aware of his triumph but, as it were, generous to the beaten enemy. “Think it over yourself, Grigory Vassilyevitch. It is said in the Scripture that if you have faith, even as a mustard seed, and tell a mountain to move into the sea, it will move at your bidding without the least delay. Well, Grigory Vassilyevitch, if I am without faith, and you have so great a faith that you are continually swearing at me, then try it yourself. Tell this mountain to move, not into the sea, for that is a long way off, but even into our stinking little river that runs at the bottom of the garden. You will see for yourself that it won’t budge, but will stay just where it is, however much you shout at it. That shows, Grigory Vassilyevitch, that you haven’t faith in the proper manner, and only abuse others about it. Again, take into consideration that in our day no one, not only you, but actually no one, from the highest person to the lowest peasant, can shove mountains into the sea—except perhaps one man in the world, or two at most, and they are most likely saving their souls in secret somewhere in the Egyptian desert, so you wouldn’t find them. If that is so, if all the rest have no faith, will God curse all the rest? That is, the population of the whole earth, except about two hermits in the desert? And in His well-known mercy, will He not forgive even one of them? And so I am persuaded that, though I may once have doubted, I shall be forgiven if I shed tears of repentance.”
“Wait!” cried Fyodor Pavlovitch, in a transport of delight. “So you do suppose there are two who can move mountains? Ivan, make a note of it, write it down. There you have the Russian all over!”
“You’re quite right to say it’s typical of the people’s faith,” Ivan agreed, with an approving smile.
“You agree. Then it must be so, if you agree. It’s true, isn’t it, Alyosha? That’s the Russian faith all over, isn’t it?”
“No, Smerdyakov has not the Russian faith at all,” said Alyosha, firm and grave.
“I’m not talking about his faith. I mean those two in the desert, only that idea. Surely that’s Russian, isn’t it?”
“Yes, that’s purely Russian,” said Alyosha, smiling.

“Your words are worth a gold piece, you ass, and I’ll give it to you today. But as for the rest, you talk nonsense, nonsense, nonsense. Let me tell you, stupid, that all of us here are of little faith, only out of carelessness, because we haven’t time. Things are too much for us. And in the second place, the Lord God has given us so little time, only twenty-four hours in the day, so that a man hasn’t even time to get enough sleep, much less to repent of his sins. While you denied your faith to your enemies when you had nothing else to think about but showing your faith! So I consider, brother, that it counts as a sin.”

“It may count as a sin, but think it over yourself, Grigory Vassilyevitch, that it only lessens the sin, if it does count as one. If I had believed then in very truth, as I ought to have believed, then it really would have been sinful if I had not faced tortures for my faith and had gone over to the pagan Mohammedan faith. But of course it would not have come to torture then, because I should only have had to say at that instant to the mountain, ‘Move and crush the tormentor,’ and it would have moved and crushed him at that very instant like a black-beetle, and I should have walked away as though nothing had happened, praising and glorifying God. But suppose that at that very moment I had tried all that, and cried to that mountain, ‘Crush these tormentors,’ and it hadn’t crushed them. How could I have helped doubting, I ask you, at such a time, in such a dreadful hour of mortal terror? And apart from that, I should know already that I could not attain to the fullness of the Kingdom of Heaven (for since the mountain had not moved at my word, they could not think very much of my faith up above, and there could be no very great reward waiting for me in the world to come). So why should I let them flay the skin off me as well, and to no good purpose? For even if they had flayed my skin half off my back, even then the mountain would not have moved at my word or at my cry. And at such a moment not only might doubt come over one, but one might lose one’s reason from fear, so that one would not be able to think at all. And so how should I be particularly to blame if, not seeing my advantage or reward either there or here, I should at least save my skin? And so, trusting fully in the grace of the Lord, I should cherish the hope that I might be altogether forgiven.”
